transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-11-20
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 49 minutes
Location: Zoom call
Attendees: Olivia Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Dana Ortiz (SE), Rachel Kim (Head of ML - Triton), Tom Alvarez (CTO - Triton), Priya Singh (Eng Mgr - Triton), Evan Park (Platform - Triton)

Summary (auto):
Discovery focused on model selection trade-offs for Triton Logistics' multimodal routing assistant. Key topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment; context-length needs (32k vs 64k); multilingual support (EN/ES/FR/DE); tool-calling / function-calling and external API integration; benchmarking and next steps to run short lat tests. Action items and follow-ups listed.

Transcript:
[00:00] Olivia Chen: Alright thanks everyone for joining, we'll give it a quick intro. I'm Olivia, AE on the Redwood side, and with me is Marcus and Dana from our solutions engineering team. Um, Rachel, Tom, Priya, Evan, thanks for carving out the time.
[00:12] Rachel Kim: Yeah thanks. We appreciate it. Quick background — we're building a routing assistant for dispatchers, multi-lingual, does ETA estimations and integrates with external telematics via tool calls. Latency is pretty important.
[00:26] Tom Alvarez: And we'd like to avoid doing model ops ourself for now, so looking at hosted first but open to dedicated or private for compliance.
[00:34] Marcus Lee: Cool. Can you share the key constraints? Like throughput, SLA, context length needs?
[00:39] Priya Singh: Throughput's medium — maybe 200 concurrent agent sessions during peak, each session sends short history plus a 10k token manifest (route state). We need support for Spanish and French, so multilingual. Also tool-calling to our internal APIs to fetch live vehicle status.
[01:02] Dana Ortiz: When you say 10k token manifest, is that total sequence length or do you expect growth to 32k?
[01:08] Priya Singh: Good question. For the first phase it's around 10 to 12k, but we want the option to go up to 32k for better context in phase two.
[01:16] Olivia Chen: Okay — that's helpful. On the Redwood side we have Hosted API which is quickest to start, Redwood Dedicated for reserved GPU capacity if you want predictable throughput and lower unit cost, and Redwood Private for VPC/on-prem for strict data controls.
[01:30] Rachel Kim: Can you speak to the model selection piece? We saw some open models that claim long context and multimodal support. How do we pick?
[01:38] Marcus Lee: Yeah, so model selection typically depends on three axes for you: context length, latency/cost tradeoff, and feature support — like function-calling/tool-calling and multilingual quality. For long context you might look at models with native 32k or 64k context windows. Some vendors provide chunking and KV-cache helpers which can emulate longer context with lower cost.
[01:56] Tom Alvarez: KV-cache helpers? Can you expand — I've seen mentions of K-V cache in some runtime docs but not sure how it works in practice.
[02:03] Marcus Lee: Sure — the K-V cache stores activations for prior tokens so you don't always re-compute the entire history. Redwood runtime does continuous batching and KV cache management. In some benchmarks that reduces per-token compute a lot, but there's still memory pressure for true 64k sequences. Also quantization affects memory and latency.
[02:21] Rachel Kim: We're sensitive to latency — aim is sub-400ms for short calls, but larger context calls can be 800-1200ms; is that realistic?
[02:29] Dana Ortiz: For hosted setups with optimized kernels, sub-400ms is doable for smaller context and smaller models. For 32k sequences you'll probably be in the 700-1500ms range depending on model and hardware. Dedicated with pinned GPU pools can give more consistent latency.
[02:42] Priya Singh: Is function-calling supported across models? We need deterministic tool calls to our telematics and ticketing APIs.
[02:49] Marcus Lee: Function-calling is supported at the API layer; the difference is model-level behavior. Some open models are better at structured outputs and adhering to function schemas. We typically recommend running a short eval on your call patterns — we can help with that benchmark spreadsheet.
[03:03] Tom Alvarez: About multilingual quality — do you recommend one large multilingual model or separate language-specific models?
[03:09] Marcus Lee: Tradeoffs: One multilingual model simplifies ops but may be slightly worse for edge languages. If you have heavy Spanish/French traffic, a multilingual model fine-tuned or a specific Spanish-specialized model can be better. We usually test with a prompt set and use Rouge/BLEU style metrics plus human evals.
[03:23] Rachel Kim: We also have compliance questions — logs, SOC 2, KMS — and whether PII is stored if using Hosted.
[03:29] Olivia Chen: For Hosted, by default we retain logs for X days for QA, but enterprise options include longer retention controls or no retention. We have SOC 2 and ISO documents — I'll share the security pack. For encryption we integrate with KMS and HSM options on the Private and Dedicated tiers; Hosted supports envelope encryption and customer-managed keys in some regions.
[03:50] Evan Park: For Private deployment, network wise we need TLS mutual auth and specific egress rules. Any experience with on-prem air-gapped installs?
[03:58] Dana Ortiz: Yes — we've done Private (on-prem) with an offline installer for regulated customers. It takes more time to stand up but gives full control. For VPC deployments, we support VPC peering and direct connect, and we can map egress ports — Marcus will note the specific requirements.
[04:14] [crosstalk] Tom Alvarez: Is there a way to fall back to smaller models if capacity spikes?
[04:18] Marcus Lee: Absolutely — Redwood's smart routing can fallback to compatible model variants by policy. Canary/A-B rollouts are supported too.
[04:25] Priya Singh: Cost — do you have an estimate comparing Hosted vs Dedicated for our expected load?
[04:29] Olivia Chen: We'll do a TCO. Quick rule of thumb: Hosted is higher unit price but no infra ops; Dedicated requires commit but reduces per-token costs at scale. We'll put numbers in the pricing deck.
[04:38] Rachel Kim: About benchmarks — we'd like Redwood to run a quick test for our key prompt set and tooling: latency, token cost, multilingual accuracy. Can you do that?
[04:46] Marcus Lee: Yep — if you send sample prompts and a small eval set we can run it on Hosted and a Dedicated config, and return a spreadsheet. We may obfuscate PII for testing if needed.
[04:56] Tom Alvarez: Any gotchas on the model side? We saw things like hallucinations on complex routing logic.
[05:01] Marcus Lee: Hallucinations are model-dependent; we recommend combined approaches — structured function calls for facts and retrieval, and using evals/QA to detect regressions. Also prompt design and system messages help.
[05:12] Rachel Kim: For tool-calling, we need guaranteed ordering and idempotency — will Redwood's function-calling guarantee that?
[05:19] Dana Ortiz: The API supports function schema and structured outputs but ordering/ idempotency is ultimately at the application layer. We can add tracing and correlation IDs to help you reconcile calls.
[05:31] Priya Singh: Regarding context expansion — you mentioned prefix caching. Can that help us keep only the last 2k tokens live and reference older context efficiently?
[05:40] Marcus Lee: Yes — prefix/KV caching can store summarized or chunked embeddings and reuse them. It's workload-specific; for routing manifests you might do vector retrieval of long-term state plus a short active context. That keeps per-token costs low.
[05:53] Tom Alvarez: Any constraints on model tool capability? For example, does a 32k model support function-calling the same as a 4k model?
[05:59] Marcus Lee: Functionally yes at the API layer, but larger-context models can behave differently because they condition on more history — sometimes that's beneficial, sometimes you need to tune the system message.
[06:10] Evan Park: On security docs — can we get SOC2 and the architecture notes?
[06:13] Olivia Chen: Yes, I'll send the security pack and a redacted SOC 2 attestation.
[06:17] Rachel Kim: Timeline — we want a POC by end of Q1. Is that feasible?
[06:21] Olivia Chen: Totally feasible. Usually a 6-8 week POC for dedicated setups, quicker for Hosted. We'll propose a plan.
[06:28] [silence/typing]
[06:35] Marcus Lee: Next up, quick notes on suggested model shortlist for your needs:
- Option A: Multilingual 32k open model (good middle ground for your 10-12k, upgradeable to 32k) — lower cost than 64k, decent multilingual PPL/quality.
- Option B: 64k context model if you want headroom and simplified architecture (higher cost, more memory).
- Option C: Smaller 8k/16k model with prefix + retrieval + KV-cache for most calls and a fallback 32k model for long sessions (cost-effective hybrid).
[06:58] Tom Alvarez: Which open models specifically?
[07:01] Marcus Lee: There are a few. Some teams test Llama variants, Mistral long-context forks, and specialised long-context models like LongRed or context-extended open weights. We can map performance to our catalog — Redwood-verified profiles — but we'd run your prompt set to confirm.
[07:18] Rachel Kim: Do you support model quantization and mixed precision to reduce instance sizes?
[07:22] Dana Ortiz: Yes, the runtime supports quantization-friendly paths; there are tradeoffs in accuracy. We'll show quant profiles and recommended knobs.
[07:30] Priya Singh: How about multi-region routing? We'll have users in NA and EU. Data residency matters for EU.
[07:36] Olivia Chen: We route by region and you can pin model instances to regions. For EU-only residency we can run private deployments in EU cloud regions and ensure logs stay in-region.
[07:46] Tom Alvarez: Any regulatory certifications for healthcare-adjacent data?
[07:49] Olivia Chen: We have enterprise compliance offerings; for regulated healthcare customers we recommend Private deployment with our enterprise package — we can go into details in the security review call.
[07:58] Rachel Kim: Great. On the integration side, we'll need sample code and an SDK for Java/Node.
[08:04] Marcus Lee: We have SDKs and examples; Marcus will drop sample snippets and a quick start repo link.
[08:11] Priya Singh: Can you also include notes on autoscaling and burst capacity for Dedicated? We might need spikes during incidents.
[08:17] Dana Ortiz: Dedicated supports configurable autoscaling and burst pools; we can include typical policy examples.
[08:23] Tom Alvarez: What's the usual SLA for Dedicated?
[08:26] Olivia Chen: SLA varies by package — we have uptime and latency targets for enterprise tiers. We'll include the SLA summary in the enterprise packet.
[08:34] [wrap-up]
[08:36] Olivia Chen: Quick recap: we'll send a pricing/TCO comparison, security pack, and benchmark spreadsheet template. Marcus will run an initial hosted benchmark if you can supply prompts. We'll schedule the technical deep dive next week to look at VPC network details.
[08:48] Rachel Kim: Sounds good. We'll send an initial prompt set and our network diagram to Evan's email.
[08:52] Tom Alvarez: Thanks all — this was helpful.
[08:54] Olivia Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the materials and times for the deep dive.

End of transcript.
